paragraphs: One-sentence judgment: this occupation is worth further verification only if you are willing to handle account permissions, backup verification, changes, and incident details over the long term, respond per process outside working hours, and accept high-consequence responsibility for production environments.

Core output: turning servers, networks, accounts, and changes into traceable operations results: configurations and baselines, monitoring and alerts, backup recoverability, access control, incident handling, and service recovery records.

20 to 120 minute safe trial: in an isolated simulation or laboratory environment (not connected to the production network, without using real credentials), complete one change-verify-rollback exercise: state the change items, impact surface, verification points, rollback conditions, and escalation path, and have someone else review against the checklist.

First threshold: first confirm the position's authorization boundaries: which operations you may perform yourself, which must go through change approval, who is responsible for release and rollback, and whether on-call or call-out duty is required; being able to log in to a system does not mean being authorized.

Network and computer systems administrators (O*NET 15-1244.00) install, configure, and maintain an organization's local area networks, wide area networks, data communication networks, operating systems, and physical and virtual servers, perform system monitoring, and verify the integrity and availability of hardware, network, and server resources.

Daily work centers on accounts and permissions, configuration changes, patches and upgrades, backup verification, log review, and incident response; output should be traceable and executed only on authorized systems and within the authorized scope.

entries: Network and host maintenance: install, configure, and maintain network devices, operating systems, and physical and virtual servers.
Monitoring and backup: monitor performance and availability, review system and application logs, and verify that scheduled tasks (including backups) complete.
Access and resource control: analyze network and server resource usage, and configure and control user access per authorization.
Software and licensing: install and upgrade software and maintain software license compliance.
Diagnosis and coordination: diagnose and resolve hardware, software, network, and system problems, replace components when necessary, and coordinate with users, vendors, and other teams.

paragraphs: The work mostly takes place indoors and is computer-based, with email the most frequent communication channel; it may involve out-of-hours change windows, on-call, or call-out duty, and the O*NET survey shows that the consequences of error are mostly serious.
Quality is measured by system availability, traceable changes, recoverable backups, compliant permissions, and incident recovery time, rather than by familiarity with a specific tool.

The common key judgments are: whether a change requires approval, what the impact surface and rollback conditions are, whether permissions exceed boundaries, whether backups are actually recoverable, and whether the logs are sufficient to support root cause analysis.

Responsibility boundary: do not bypass change approval and security controls; operations involving production environments, personal information, and regulated systems must be performed within the authorized scope and record requirements, and control requirements should be tailored to the organization's scope.

The work loop in order is: receive a request or alert → assess impact and authorization → perform the change or handling → verify results and backup recoverability → record and hand over; occupational boundary: this occupation is not the same as network architects, information security analysts, or software developers.

Network architects: responsible for designing target network architecture, capacity, and technology selection, leaning toward plans and planning; this occupation leans toward operations, maintenance, and incident handling in production environments.
Computer network support specialists: focus more on support response for end users and network problems, with a scope usually narrower than full system and server operations.
Computer systems analysts: focus more on business system requirements and solution design, with different responsibility for day-to-day production changes than this occupation.

Selection signal: do not compare only that all of them touch computers or networks; compare the authorization scope, on-call and change responsibility, whether security and compliance records are required, and the industry and employer type.
Adjacent directions include: computer-network-architects, computer-network-support-specialists, computer-systems-analysts, information-security-analysts, database-administrators

Break down the tasks first: generative AI task exposure is not equal to actual adoption, automation probability, or job disappearance; this page uses only O*NET task and tool evidence for item-by-item analysis and does not invent a replacement rate for this occupation.

Editorial analysis (subject to authorization, de-identification, and test conditions): better suited for assistance: log summarization and anomaly clustering, listing failure hypotheses, script or command drafts, first drafts of change descriptions and operating documents, and ticket classification.

Retrieval assistance: can help look up configuration item meanings, error codes, and vendor documentation; versions, applicable environments, and conclusions must be manually verified, and O*NET employer technology signals only indicate mention rates, not the degree of automation.

Editorial analysis (subject to authorization, de-identification, and test conditions): risk screening assistance: can flag configuration drift, overly broad permissions, or missing backups, but cannot replace actual scanning, change approval, and release decisions.

Must not be delegated to AI: directly performing changes in production environments, deciding release or rollback, handling security incidents, granting or revoking permissions, or bypassing approval.

Human control points: verify assets and configurations, confirm the impact surface and rollback, execute change approval, verify backup recoverability, confirm least privilege, and keep auditable records.

Data threshold: process the minimum necessary information only in authorized systems; logs, configurations, and account information must not be entered into unauthorized external models or tools, and privacy and audit rules must be followed.

Ability exercise (editorial suggestion): practice troubleshooting reasoning, rollback design, recovery verification, log analysis, and collaborative record keeping; no comparative study was obtained showing it outperforms the speed of generating commands.

Insufficient evidence: no national Chinese occupational wage distribution under the same scope as O*NET15-1244 was obtained this round, and no one-to-one classification mapping was verified. The information technology industry average is only a reference for employers in that industry, and finance, education, manufacturing, and government IT positions cannot all apply it directly.

Scope comparison: the National Bureau of Statistics of China publishes average wages of urban unit employees by industry category and does not list network and computer systems administrators separately.

Checkable reference: in 2025 the average annual wage for information transmission, software, and information technology services was 248,752 yuan per year for urban non-private units and 128,166 yuan per year for urban private units in the same category; the statistical scope is urban legal entities with 5 or more employees and excludes self-employed individuals and freelancers.

Insufficient evidence: no Chinese occupational wage distribution under the same scope was obtained this round; industry averages cannot be used to infer percentiles or individual income for this occupation. Verify the specific city, contract, on-call arrangements, hours, pay, and authorization requirements; an industry proxy does not replace a written employer quote.
The 2025 BLS OEWS national median shown by O*NET is 47.66 USD per hour and 99,130 USD per year; the page marks it as the exact occupation 15-1244.00 scope, not starting pay or a personal quote.

The national percentile annual wages under the same scope are: 10th percentile 62,640 USD, 25th percentile 78,010 USD, 75th percentile 126,640 USD, and 90th percentile 155,050 USD (corresponding hourly rates 30.11, 37.51, 60.89, and 74.55 USD).
Percentiles and the median all use the 2025 BLS OEWS national scope and cannot be directly compared across years, regions, or occupations.

OEWS is a wage statistic for employees of non-farm establishments and excludes self-employment; independent contractor income and employee wages cannot be compared together. Specific bonuses, overtime, on-call, and equity items must be verified against employer quotes, and it cannot be generalized that all contract workers are excluded.
A low percentile is not starting pay, and distribution data cannot be used to estimate individual take-home pay or after-tax income.

Actual pay should be verified against the specific employer, industry, region, and position level; United States figures cannot be converted into or extrapolated as individual income in mainland China.

Caution signal: you tend to bypass approval for quick fixes, or treat being able to log in as being authorized to perform changes.

paragraphs: Caution signal: you are drawn mainly by technical interest but are unwilling to carry production environment responsibility, audit records, and continuous learning of system and security requirements.

Verification method: personality labels cannot determine fit; use change-verify-rollback exercises, log analysis, and handover explanations in an isolated simulation environment to be evaluated by experienced staff.

Service interruption: a change or failure makes a critical system unavailable; the consequence is business interruption and higher recovery costs; the controls are change approval, impact assessment, and a rollback plan. Unrecoverable backups: the backup job shows success but cannot actually be restored; the consequence is data loss; the controls are periodic restore drills and off-site copies. Overly broad or abusive permissions: account permissions exceed duties or accounts are shared long term; the consequence is data leakage and audit failure; the controls are least privilege, periodic review, and privileged monitoring. Configuration drift and shadow assets: unregistered devices or configurations deviating from the baseline; the consequence is a larger exposure surface and harder fault localization; the controls are an asset inventory and configuration baseline verification. Delayed patching and supply chain: patches not applied in time or unevaluated third-party components introduced; the consequence is exploitation and compliance problems; the controls are a patching process and change assessment.

Boundary statement: this list cannot replace the organization's security systems, change management, privacy, and audit requirements; when production environments, personal information, and regulated systems are involved, act per actual authorization and process, and tailor control requirements to the organization's scope.

Direct answer: the main risks in this occupation come from service interruption, unrecoverable backups, permission overreach, configuration drift, and delayed patching; control depends on change approval, least privilege, restore drills, and traceable records.

Affected roles: operations staff responsible for production changes, account permissions, and backup recovery; the consequences of error are equally serious early in the job, so escalation chains and record requirements are not relaxed by seniority.

Possible consequences (editorial scenario): critical service interruption, business loss, and recovery costs; O*NET tasks and the error consequence survey support the risk premise, and NIST general controls must be tailored per institution, without proving a fixed incidence rate or legal penalty.

Step 0: determine the organization and authorization scope. First clarify the employer's technology stack, production environment responsibility boundaries, change and on-call systems, and whether specific security or compliance training is required; the path on this page is an editorial synthesis, does not represent uniform entry conditions, and does not constitute any system authorization.

Practice takes place only in an isolated simulation or laboratory environment: not connected to the production network, without using real account credentials, and without performing real changes; the simulation environment and data should be disposable, and their source and version recorded.

The portfolio includes: a simulated change request (impact surface, verification points, rollback conditions), a backup restore drill record, log analysis conclusions, and permission list verification results; it contains no real hostnames, accounts, or user data.

Verify certifications, product versions, and organizational permissions against the target position.

Ability progression starts with stable ticket execution and records, then takes on complete changes, root cause analysis, and backup recovery responsibility, and finally takes part in standards development and cross-team collaboration; daily operations, change approval, and security release remain separated by role authorization throughout.

entries.answer: According to O*NET 15-1244.00, this occupation installs, configures, and maintains local area networks, wide area networks, data communication networks, operating systems, and physical and virtual servers, monitors systems and scheduled tasks, verifies backup completion, analyzes resource usage, and controls user access, and also diagnoses and resolves hardware, software, network, and system failures.

entries.answer: Network architects are responsible for designing target network architecture and capacity planning, leaning toward plans and long-term selection; computer network support specialists focus more on support response for end users and network problems; this occupation focuses on operations, maintenance, changes, and incident handling in production environments, and carries daily responsibility for accounts, backups, and server resources.

components.definition_block: Network and computer systems administrators (O*NET 15-1244.00) install, configure, and maintain an organization's local area networks, wide area networks, data communication networks, operating systems, and physical and virtual servers, perform monitoring, verify backups and scheduled tasks, analyze resource usage, and control user access; the actual scope that can be performed is determined by employer authorization, change management, and security requirements.

fermat_decision_card.summary: In an isolated simulation environment, do one change-verify-rollback exercise: state the change items, impact surface, verification points, rollback conditions, and escalation path, and also do one backup restore drill and permission list verification, then ask experienced staff for feedback; the exercise does not constitute system authorization, change approval, or an employer hiring promise.
fermat_decision_card.title: Network and computer systems administrators

hero.quick_answer: Network and computer systems administrators (O*NET 15-1244.00) install, configure, and maintain an organization's local area networks, wide area networks, data communication networks, operating systems, and physical and virtual servers, monitor the integrity and availability of systems and scheduled tasks (including backups), analyze network and server resource usage and control user access, and may also assist with network modeling, analysis, and planning coordination. This page uses only official sources to explain the occupation scope, tasks, preparation requirements, Chinese and United States statistical scopes, and authorization boundaries.

description.text: Network and computer systems administrators (O*NET 15-1244.00) install, configure, and maintain an organization's local area networks, wide area networks, data communication networks, operating systems, and physical and virtual servers, monitor the integrity and availability of systems and scheduled tasks (including backups), analyze network and server resource usage and control user access, and may also assist with network modeling, analysis, and planning coordination. This page uses only official sources to explain the occupation scope, tasks, preparation requirements, Chinese and United States statistical scopes, and authorization boundaries.
